std::atomic_ref<T>

workaround. Also rewrote the store serialization for tx. This allocates all inputs and all outputs in one chunk each, and writes them contiguously, as opposed to iterating over the allocation. Given that input/output both cache size during wired deserialization there's no cost to computing the variable offsets. I also found that I was using the script and witness size methods previously, to store the size prefixes. But those aren't cached, so that was a bit wasteful - iteration over all opcodes. So allocations are reduced by around 5 billion or so, and those impose an exclusive lock over respective tables, which is the only material source of lock contention, so that's really good.

elements.text: The other is the double spend query, which can run entirely concurrent across blocks (except for the rare encountered possible double spend). This is heavily store intensive (SSD/RAM) with very low CPU, which is why it runs so cheaply on the maxi. However completing it on the mini with nothing else running, sequentially by block, still maxes out SSD from the start. The reason it starts hard is the isolated run starts with tables fully populated, so all queries are max paging cost due to max conflicts. There are only three tables involved, the tx table (to get the hash, no search required), the point table (search for point matches), and the prevout table (which is read in sequential chunks by block, and contains all point indexes and parent tx ids). I just realized that the change the point table from "foreign point" - a 7 byte search key consisting of the point.hash primary key and the 3 byte point.index, resulted in a dramatic increase in hashmap collisions in the point table. The new point table search key is the full 32 byte sha256 hash and the 3 byte index. Since the original pk's were guaranteed to be unique, point table collisions were almost zero. Now they are more normally distributed. However, previously to obtain the fp, one had to search the input table for the sha256 hash.

So it's ultimately better, but there is an aspect of it that I hadn't measured before. Combining the dual key previously was effective, because of the uniqueness of the pk. But combining the lower 8 bytes of the sha256 hash and the sequential point index for identical point.hashes was not previously measured, and it's very weak. Which means one of the issues has been long collision chains. I'll measure the actual rate with the old combiner and a more effective one. Since the combiner is only used in this one table, it can pay to have more computation and reduce the rate. Prob not huge, but definitely material.

elements.text: So it's been nagging me that this should be doable with positive (no delete) accumulation during download, across download threads, in a lock-free manner, without having to search the point table at all. So I worked through some statistical accumulation options, and had Grok do some sizing. I also pulled out the actual conflict rates in the point table, as this is critical for the estimation. I looked at Bloom and Cuckoo filtering, and settled on Bloom because it's far more space efficient because it doesn't support deletion - which we don't need. Either can be performed concurrently in a lock free manner, though Bloom is a little more complex to do so. Cuckoo would be basically using our hashmap header template, and its memory fencing. Bloom requires striping the filter by thread (basically independent filters, sharding the space). Bloom also requires more computation, but that's pretty trivial.

elements.text: So going with Bloom, it comes down to a straightforward tradeoff between filter size and false positive rate. There are no false negatives, but false positives are like hash conflicts and increase as the filter saturates. These can only be resolved by querying the main point table, which of course we want to avoid. Increasing filter size is like increasing table headers. Headers and the filter are randomly accessed and therefore consume most of their size in RAM. Currently the total header set is 16GB, and I'm looking at 4GB more for the initial filter sizing. That eats about 20GB RAM. The reset is preserved for working and paging space as blocks are downloaded, read, populated, and validated. As we are filtering in the construction of the table, the LF starts at 1 and progresses (e.g. to 1.5) as the table populates. Given the presumption of almost no duplicates ("true positives"), the FP rate indicates the ratio of body searches to inserts while building the table. The FP rate is a non-linear monotonically increasing function of the LF. Basically like any hash function, an increasing load factor increases the search cost from constant toward linear.

            bit_or
            (
                bit_and(print, mask),
                bit_and(sieve, bit_not(mask))

text: Switched the hashmap heads back to modulo truncation today, so got granular control over sizing. Ran a mini milestone run with all hashmaps LF 1.5 (previous points table was 2.446). This change was projected to reduce search to ~25% of previous, and after this run I measured an average rate of `0.14%` vs. `0.53%` with the higher load factor, so right on. This also drops the late stage LF by the same amount, so from `1.1%` of inserts, to `0.29%`. This is significant, and all comes at the cost of increasing the heads by `2.2GiB`. We won't see the impact of that until tomorrow morning. The total head size for validation will be `18.2GiB`, whereas in yesterday's high LF run it was `16.0GiB`. The earlier run that bogged down with a `1.22LF` was too big, at `24GiB` heads. So I'm hopeful that this will be much better, but in any case we should be able to squeeze enough out of the heads to get to yesterday's `16.0GiB` if we have to, and that will certainly be good.

elements.text:
The reason this helps confirmation is that double spends are rare. In our use they consist of conflicting unconfirmed txs, race condition duplicates, valid duplicates (2 from bip30), and actually strong branch invalid block tx duplications (the ones we need to check for). So by recording these rare duplicates we can reduce the double spend query cost to almost zero for block-inclusions.

Compact blocks will absorb existing txs, so they won't benefit from this exclusion (two valid blocks can spend the same tx record). However this is only a performance issue during sync. A single block full double spend query is very fast. And it will continue to work  for catch-up sync (i.e. after compacts have come in) as well.
